content: If the platelet count falls below 25 x 10^9/L, or if severe adverse reactions occur, the dose should be reduced by 50% or temporarily withheld until the adverse reactions subside. If intolerance persists, the treatment should be permanently discontinued. Regular monitoring of liver function tests (LFTs), complete blood count (CBC), platelets, hemoglobin (Hgb), electrolytes, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is recommended. When used in combination with ribavirin, the initial dose is 3 million units/m² administered intramuscularly (IM) or subcutaneously (SC) three times per week for one week. This can be increased to 6 million units/m² SC three times per week for 16–24 weeks, but the dose should not exceed 10 million units per dose three times per week. Dose adjustments should follow the manufacturer’s package insert. Interferon alfa-2b increases the levels or effects of fezolinetant by altering hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 metabolism, making the combination contraindicated. Fezolinetant’s area under the curve (AUC) and peak plasma concentration are elevated when co-administered with weak, moderate, or strong CYP1A2 inhibitors, including interferon alfa-2b and deferiprone. These combinations increase toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy and should be avoided or replaced with alternative drugs. If deferiprone must be used, monitor the absolute neutrophil count more frequently due to the risk of neutropenia or agranulocytosis. Palifermin increases the toxicity of interferon alfa-2b and should not be administered within 24 hours before, during, or after the infusion of antineoplastic agents. Co-administration within this timeframe has been associated with increased severity and duration of oral mucositis. Similarly, pexidartinib, which can cause hepatotoxicity, should not be co-administered with other hepatotoxic agents, including interferon alfa-2b. Pretomanid, which is associated with hepatotoxicity, should also be avoided in combination with interferon alfa-2b. Patients on pretomanid should avoid alcohol, hepatotoxic agents, and herbal supplements. Ropinterferon alfa-2b and interferon alfa-2b can cause additive myelosuppression, necessitating close monitoring for excessive myelosuppression. Similarly, acalabrutinib and interferon alfa-2b may increase myelosuppressive effects, requiring caution and monitoring. Hydroxyurea, when used with interferon alfa-2b, has been associated with cutaneous vasculitic toxicities, such as vasculitic ulcerations and gangrene, particularly in patients with a history of interferon therapy. Lamivudine combined with interferon alfa-2b increases the risk of liver decompensation, requiring caution and monitoring. Ponesimod and siponimod, when combined with interferon alfa-2b, increase immunosuppressive effects and the risk of infection. Caution is advised during co-administration and in the weeks following therapy. When switching from drugs with prolonged immune effects, consider their half-life and mechanism of action to avoid unintended additive immunosuppression. Interferon alfa-2b increases the levels of theophylline by reducing its metabolism, with a greater risk of interaction in smokers. Tobramycin (inhaled) and interferon alfa-2b both increase nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity risks, so concurrent or sequential use should be avoided. Ublituximab and interferon alfa-2b may cause additive immunosuppressive effects, increasing the risk of infection. Close monitoring is required when these drugs are co-administered. Interferon alfa-2b enhances the effects of warfarin through an unspecified mechanism, necessitating caution and monitoring. It also increases zidovudine levels by reducing its metabolism, requiring similar precautions. Shark cartilage, when combined with interferon alfa-2b, may theoretically enhance anti-angiogenesis effects, though the clinical significance is unknown. Weight loss and growth inhibition have been reported in pediatric patients receiving combination therapy with interferon alfa-2b. Long-term growth inhibition (height) has been observed in some cases. Peripheral neuropathy has been noted when used with telbivudine. There is a risk of visual impairment and retinal disorders; treatment should be discontinued if ophthalmologic problems develop. Use caution in patients with endocrine disorders, such as thyroid disease or diabetes mellitus prone to ketoacidosis, as well as those with pre-existing cardiac abnormalities or advanced cancer. Interferon alfa-2b should not be used in patients with AIDS-related Kaposi’s sarcoma who have rapidly progressive disease. Treatment should be discontinued if acute hypersensitivity occurs. There is a risk of exacerbating pre-existing psoriasis and sarcoidosis or developing new sarcoidosis. Patients should remain well-hydrated during initial treatment. If platelet counts fall below 50,000/mm³, avoid intramuscular administration and consider subcutaneous administration instead. The 18 million IU or 50 million IU powder for injection and the 18 million IU multidose vial should not be used for condylomata acuminata. Interferon alfa-2b increases the risk of hepatic decompensation and death in patients with cirrhosis. Any patient developing liver function abnormalities during treatment should be closely monitored, and treatment should be discontinued if necessary. Cardiotoxicities, including arrhythmias, ischemia, infarction, and cardiomyopathy, have been reported during and immediately after infusion. Interferon alfa-2b is classified as Pregnancy Category C, meaning risk to the fetus cannot be ruled out. Its safety during lactation is unknown.
